lesson.title: No Memory Required: The Logic Behind Stateless Protocols
lesson.summary: A stateless protocol treats every request as a self-contained transaction that carries all the context it needs, so the server never has to remember what happened before, a design choice that trades built-in continuity for simplicity and massive scalability.
lesson.body:
A protocol is just an agreed set of rules for how two systems exchange messages, but protocols differ sharply in how much history they expect either side to remember. A stateless protocol is one where each request from a client to a server is handled entirely on its own terms. The server does not retain any memory of prior requests from that client, and nothing about how request number five is processed depends on what happened in requests one through four. Every message must be self-describing: it has to include whatever information is needed to process it, because the receiving end has no stored context to fall back on.

This is closely related to, but distinct from, the idea of a connectionless service. Connectionless describes whether a persistent communication channel is set up before data flows, the way UDP sends datagrams without any handshake, while stateless describes whether the protocol logic itself remembers anything across separate exchanges. A protocol can run on top of a connection-oriented transport and still be stateless in its own right. HTTP is the textbook case: each HTTP request is processed independently by the web server's application logic even though the underlying TCP connection carrying it is very much stateful, tracking sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and window sizes for as long as the connection stays open.

The reason statelessness matters so much in practice is scalability and resilience. If a server keeps no memory of clients between requests, then any server in a pool can handle any incoming request, which is exactly what lets a load balancer spread traffic across dozens or thousands of interchangeable machines without worrying about routing a given client back to its own server. It also makes failure recovery simple: if a stateless server crashes and restarts, no client session is lost, because there was never any session stored there to begin with.

DNS is a clean real-world example. When a resolver asks a DNS server to look up a domain name, that query contains everything the server needs: the name being queried, the record type, and enough identifying information to match a reply to the request. The DNS server answers and immediately forgets the exchange ever happened. The next query, even from the same client, gets no special treatment or shortcut based on the previous one.

Of course, real applications often need continuity, like keeping a user logged in across many page loads, and stateless protocols do not forbid this, they just push the responsibility elsewhere. HTTP servers commonly stay stateless while the client carries a cookie or authentication token with every request, effectively smuggling the needed context along inside each self-contained message rather than asking the server to remember it.

This is not an accident of history either. When Roy Fielding formally described REST, the architectural style behind most modern web APIs, in his year 2000 doctoral dissertation, statelessness was one of the small set of constraints he named explicitly, precisely because of the scalability and reliability benefits it produces. A well-designed REST API endpoint should be usable by swapping in any backend server at any moment, with no request depending on which specific server handled the one before it, which is the same idea DNS and basic HTTP already embody at a smaller scale.
